text: The Gödel Prize is an annual award given jointly by the European Association for Theoretical Computer Science (EATCS) and the Association for Computing Machinery Special Interest Group on Algorithms and Computational Theory (ACM SIGACT) for outstanding papers in theoretical computer science. The prize is named in honor of Kurt Gödel, who first introduced the "P versus NP" question in a 1956 letter to John von Neumann, asking whether a certain NP-complete problem could be solved in quadratic or linear time. First awarded in 1993, the prize is presented alternately at ICALP (in even years) and STOC (in odd years), with STOC being the ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, a leading North American conference in theoretical computer science, and ICALP being the International Colloquium on Automata, Languages and Programming, a major European conference in the field. To qualify, a paper must be published in a refereed journal within the last 14 years (previously 7 years). The prize includes a US$5000 reward. A committee of six members selects the winner, with the EATCS President and the SIGACT Chair each appointing three members to serve staggered three-year terms, and the committee is chaired alternately by representatives of EATCS and SIGACT. In contrast to the Gödel Prize, which honors outstanding papers, the Knuth Prize is awarded to individuals for their overall impact in the field. The prize was awarded in 2004, 2011, 2013, and 2014, corresponding to papers 32, 34, 35, and 36, respectively.
